body.text: Economic resilience has become a top priority amid heightened geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation and major supply chain disruptions. For ASEAN, supply chain resilience is a critical pillar of economic resilience due to the importance of supply chain trade in the region.

However, ASEAN member states’ (AMS) participation in global value chains (GVCs) varies considerably. Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam have GVC participation rates above the ASEAN average, while Lao PDR, Indonesia and Myanmar are below. Recent data indicates that participation rates have increased for almost all the AMS but disparities remain, with Singapore maintaining its lead and Myanmar still lagging furthest (Figure 1). The former being resource-poor and small, focusing on niche production processes; while the latter is mainly manufacturing labour-intensive products such as garments, which have low domestic value additions.

ASEAN’s participation is predominantly through backward linkages, or the use of imports to produce exports. The latest data shows that this holds true for all AMS, with the exception of Myanmar and Laos (Figure 2). Forward linkage, which involves the export of intermediate inputs to trading partners for use in their export production, comprise a smaller portion. GVC participation remains concentrated in manufacturing followed by services, due to the large presence of manufacturing foreign direct investment (FDI), which shapes ASEAN participation in global supply chains.

Another important feature of ASEAN’s value chains is their primarily global, rather than regional, orientation. The low seven per cent regional value chain (RVC) participation rate indicates limited integration of production networks within ASEAN. Most of the imported inputs used to produce ASEAN’s exports originate from outside the region, and exports for downstream processing are absorbed by supply chains beyond ASEAN. This points to considerable scope for strengthening intra-regional production linkages. Increasing regional content in a supply chain strengthens regional resilience by reducing exposure to long-distance bottlenecks and geopolitical shocks.

ASEAN’s changing trade and production relationships with China and the United States add another dimension to its vulnerabilities. Based on OECD Trade in Value-added (TiVA) data, China overtook the United States as ASEAN’s dominant source of industrial inputs in 2003 and as its main industrial output destination in 2011, even before the first set of Trump tariffs occurred in 2018. In 1995, ASEAN’s dependence on US industrial inputs was three times greater than its dependence on Chinese inputs. By 2020, this relationship had reversed, with Chinese inputs exceeding the US’ by a factor of five.

A similar reversal occurred on the export side, based on the same data set — in 1995, ASEAN relied on the US market eight times more than on China. By 2020, ASEAN’s reliance on China’s market had shifted to almost 1.5 times the region’s reliance on the US. In 2024, China’s share of total trade in ASEAN was about double that of the US (Figure 3). ASEAN imported from China more than triple what it imported from the US, while China’s share in ASEAN exports was slightly lower, at 15 per cent, compared with the US’ 16 per cent.

These developments have become more consequential amid escalating China-US trade tensions. ASEAN’s trade surplus increased from 2024 to 2025, despite the imposition of Trump’s liberation day tariffs in February 2025 (Figure 4).

In fact, ASEAN’s share of the US trade deficit increased from 19 per cent in 2024 to 26.5 per cent in 2025, making it the largest regional contributor. This could expose ASEAN economies to greater US scrutiny, particularly over trade imbalances, transshipment and the origin of goods. ASEAN’s position as an intermediary in global production networks therefore presents both opportunities and vulnerabilities.

How are firms responding to Trumps’s tariffs and heightened geopolitical uncertainty? A 2025 survey by the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia (ERIA) provides three important insights. First, firms are diversifying and regionalising their supply chains in response to overlapping uncertainties. However, adjustments are generally gradual and path-dependent, shaped by existing production networks rather than large-scale relocation. Second, faced with the compounded challenge of adapting to multiple and reinforcing uncertainties, firms are depending significantly on internal capabilities and available resources. Third, firms more exposed to these uncertainties emphasise the need for coordinated regional policy responses over ad hoc national measures, particularly to strengthen medium- and long-term resilience.

The last response indicates a need for regional cooperation to overcome the supply chain disruptions created by geopolitical uncertainty. But the priority should not be more institutional layering, or the repetitive addition of new bodies, treaties, and frameworks without retiring old ones. Instead, greater attention should instead be directed to “more action” by consolidating existing initiatives and improving implementation.

In this regard, ASEAN should undertake a systematic stocktake of existing supply chain resilience initiatives, accounting for progress made and identifying implementation gaps. For instance, the Framework on ASEAN Supply Chain Efficiency and Resilience aims to enhance ASEAN’s competitiveness by lowering supply chain costs and improving speed, reliability and resilience, through five interventions: cross-border harmonisation, reduction of non-tariff barriers to trade, supply chain integration, digital supply chain promotion and industrial innovation.

Equally important is effective implementation of the ASEAN GVC Work Plan 2026–2030, with a shift towards more selective and integrated value chain cooperation. Rather than pursuing broad-based integration across all sectors, the Work Plan suggests prioritising strategic value chains such as semiconductors — for which ASEAN is developing a regional roadmap as a Priority Economic Deliverable (PED) under the Philippines’ 2026 ASEAN Chairmanship.

Finally, strengthening regional resilience via a whole of community approach, as articulated in the October 2024 ASEAN Leaders’ Declaration, would strive for firms in all members states to participate more substantively in value chains, regionally and globally. Ultimately, ASEAN’s resilience will be enhanced by stronger regional production capabilities and reduced vulnerabilities arising from uneven integration into global value chains.
